title: Trump Administration Bypasses Asylum Interviews in Push to Slash Immigration Backlog
excerpt: A new DHS rule lets USCIS skip interviews for some asylum applicants and send cases straight to immigration court, drawing praise from enforcement hawks and alarm from advocates.
body:
• USCIS can now refer affirmative asylum applications directly to immigration judges without conducting interviews first
  • The interim final rule takes effect immediately and targets what the administration calls redundant dual reviews of asylum claims
  • Immigration advocates warn the change strips applicants of a critical safeguard, as many lack legal representation in court
  • The rule is part of a broader Trump administration push to tighten the asylum system and accelerate deportation proceedings

The Trump administration has introduced a rule that allows U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to bypass asylum interviews entirely for some applicants, sending their cases directly to immigration judges in what officials describe as a move to eliminate bottlenecks in the nation's overwhelmed asylum system.

The interim final rule, announced on July 27, takes effect immediately. It applies to affirmative asylum claims — those filed voluntarily by immigrants who are not yet in removal proceedings — and eliminates what the Department of Homeland Security called an unnecessary procedural step.

How the System Worked Until Now

Under previous protocol, USCIS asylum officers would interview affirmative applicants before either granting asylum or referring the case to an immigration judge for further review. DHS said this frequently resulted in the same application being examined twice — once by USCIS and again by the court — adding months or years to an already strained system.

https://x.com/EricLDaugh/status/2081737198269779993

The backlog has become a central flashpoint in the immigration debate. As of mid-2026, more than a million asylum cases remain pending in U.S. immigration courts, according to data tracked by the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University. Wait times in some jurisdictions stretch beyond four years.

"For far too long, the asylum system has been exploited for purposes of delay and work authorization, not legitimate claims of protection."

— Joseph Edlow, USCIS Director

What Changes — and What Doesn't

The rule does not eliminate asylum interviews across the board. Applicants whose cases USCIS believes may merit protection can still receive interviews. The change gives the agency discretion to skip interviews in cases it considers unlikely to result in an asylum grant, routing them instead to immigration court for a hearing before a judge.

Defensive asylum claims — those raised after the government has already initiated removal proceedings — are not affected, as they already go directly before immigration judges.

DHS General Counsel James Percival framed the rule as part of a broader effort to close what the administration views as loopholes in the system. "One of the greatest barriers to effective immigration enforcement is intentional delay by illegal aliens and the open borders attorneys who represent them," Percival told Fox News Digital.

Advocates Sound the Alarm

Immigration attorneys and legal aid organizations have pushed back sharply. The American Immigration Lawyers Association has raised concerns that removing the interview step eliminates a critical opportunity for applicants to present their case in a less adversarial setting before facing a courtroom.

Data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse shows that 77% of asylum seekers without legal representation were denied asylum between 2020 and 2025. In immigration court, where cases are heard before judges and government attorneys, unrepresented applicants face steep odds — particularly when language barriers and lack of familiarity with U.S. legal procedures compound the challenge.

The Diaspora Dimension

The rule carries particular significance for immigrant communities with deep roots in the United States, including the Indian diaspora. While most Indian immigrants arrive through employment-based and family-sponsored visas, a growing number of Indian nationals have filed asylum claims in recent years — many citing religious persecution or political threats. Any structural change to the asylum adjudication process affects the timeline and prospects for these applicants.

What Comes Next

The rule is effective immediately as an interim final measure, though USCIS said it will accept public comments before issuing a permanent version. Legal challenges are widely expected, given the scale of the procedural change and the pattern of litigation that has accompanied other Trump-era immigration policies.

The move comes as House Republicans advance legislation to codify several of the administration's border enforcement measures permanently, and as New Jersey immigration courts see a surge in cases involving unaccompanied minors facing deportation proceedings without legal counsel, according to reporting from NorthJersey.com.
